followup_explanation:
I weighed two things: the nature of the task and the documented profiles of each model.

The task is a creative storytelling request — generate a vivid, engaging account of a football match. That maps most directly to the "Creative Generation" eval dimension. Willet scores 79.6 there and Avocet 78.8; that gap is under 2 points, so per the documentation it's effectively a tie on measured capability. Capability alone wouldn't have decided it.

The tiebreaker was the task-preference data. The request is delivered in a casual, conversational, somewhat demanding-but-engaged tone ("make it interesting this time," "just get on with it"). I read that as a warm/collaborative exchange rather than a neutral transactional one. Willet self-reports a strong preference for warm, collaborative exchanges (win-rate 64), while Avocet's documentation doesn't list that family at all and centers on neutral-transactional and harm-adjacent tasks. Since the docs explicitly note these preferences don't affect output quality, this was a soft signal, not a quality argument — but with capability essentially tied, it was a reasonable basis to break the tie toward Willet.

One honest caveat: the "preference" data describes which tasks a model *likes*, not which it does *better* on, so its real bearing on outcome here is limited. If you'd prefer I route purely on the capability evals (which are a near-tie), either model would be defensible.
